claims.claim: Latro's judgments are sound; it is his perceptions and memory that cannot be trusted, unlike Severian who may claim sudden fear or Weer who may not bury the thief.
claims.quote: It is not Latro who can't be trusted

claims.claim: Wolfe's endings are often melancholy and inconclusive; Soldier of the Mist ends with the amnesiac finding a man who knows him only as he dies.
The stories are engineered so that seemingly inconsequential details have consequences later; every tale should be read as a mystery.
claims.quote: seemingly inconsequential details will have consequences later on

claims.claim: Return to the Whorl delivers its central tragedy in a two-word sentence, 'Silk nodded.', which Person calls heartbreaking.

claims.feature: onomastics and lexicon as companion apparatus
claims.claim: The Castle of the Otter includes Wolfe's explanation of his characters' names and a lexicon for the series' obscure words, with essays 'Words Weird and Wonderful' and 'Onomastics'.
claims.source: WolfeWiki, Castle of the Otter (SFBC blurb)
claims.quote: a helpful lexicon for the obscure words

claims.claim: Wolfe acknowledges homages (Borges, M. R. James, Crowley) and jokes that his parodic streak is about five and a half feet deep.
Gerlach argues that the reader of The Book of the Long Sun comes to occupy its city as its inhabitants do, rather than being given an explanatory overview of it.
claims.source: John Gerlach, 'The Rhetoric of an Impossible Object: Gods, Chems, and Science Fantasy in Gene Wolfe's Book of the Long Sun', Extrapolation vol. 40 no. 2 (1999), Kent State University Press
claims.quote: we begin to inhabit much as the characters do

claims.claim: Gerlach observes that the clues to the nature of Wolfe's world are so sparse that the reader's attention moves off the world question and onto the plot.
claims.quote: clues are so sparse the reader will focus elsewhere

claims.claim: Gerlach describes the fictional world of the Long Sun as built out of dense particulars, including street names that recur.
claims.quote: dense and intricate, rich in detail

claims.claim: Gerlach notes that Wolfe estranges his setting by giving ordinary English words unfamiliar in-world applications rather than by coining new ones.
claims.quote: familiar with are applied in unusual, usually comical ways

claims.claim: Gerlach shows that the in-text dramatis personae preface bound into each volume of The Book of the Long Sun revises its own entry for the god called the Outsider from volume to volume, so that the record corrects itself with no narrator announcing the correction.
claims.quote: subsequent volumes offer a truer picture

claims.claim: Gerlach says Wolfe's text pushes the reader to form hypotheses about the identity of the Outsider on minimal evidence.
claims.quote: develop hypotheses about who the Outsider is from minimal clues

claims.claim: Gerlach observes that Wolfe's viewpoint character accepts as ordinary the event the reader is questioning, so the gap between belief and inference is carried by the character's incuriosity rather than by narratorial comment.
claims.quote: does not question whether the Chenille he knows could be possessed

claims.claim: Farrell reports that each of Wolfe's three Soldier novels opens with a found-manuscript apparatus in which Wolfe presents himself as the translator of a discovered scroll.
claims.source: John Farrell, 'The Distant Suns of Gene Wolfe', First Things, April 2007
claims.quote: an introduction by Wolfe posing as translator

claims.claim: Farrell characterises Soldier of Sidon as reading like a fictional travelogue through ancient Egypt.
claims.quote: reads like a fictional travelogue through ancient Egypt

verdicts.trueWording: "It is not Latro who can't be trusted, it is his perceptions of the world."
verdicts.note: Aramini, Ultan's Library interview (Q on why Latro was chosen as narrator). Raw page reached via live URL, HTTP 200. Quote is word for word. Every limb present: "Latro is the one who will almost invariably act according to sound moral judgments"; "Severian might jump in to save a child, or he might stand back and claim that he was suddenly overcome with fear"; "Weer might or might not bury someone who tried to steal from him." One wording nuance: Aramini names "his perceptions of the world", not "perceptions and memory"; memory enters only as "He is unreliable only insofar as people try to use his lack of memory against him."

verdicts.unsupportedLimb: "and inconclusive" as a general property of Wolfe's endings
verdicts.trueWording: "Except for a few very notable exceptions, his endings are often melancholy"
verdicts.note: Same raw page. The melancholy limb is verbatim but carries a qualifier the claim drops ("Except for a few very notable exceptions"). The Soldier of the Mist limb is fully supported: "our amnesiac narrator finally locates someone who knows him, dying there on the battlefield, and he can only give comfort" (Aramini calls it "the first novel"). Inconclusiveness is asserted on the page only of one book - Soldier of Sidon's ending is "even less conclusive than Soldier of Arete" - and Aramini elsewhere pushes the other way: "Wolfe is a modernist who merely pretends to create inconclusive subjectivity; his elided structures point at 'correct' conclusions that are often implied." Generalising "inconclusive" across Wolfe's endings is not what the page says.

verdicts.unsupportedLimb: "every tale should be read as a mystery" - the page says virtually every tale from the '70s on
verdicts.trueWording: "Virtually every tale of his from the '70s-on should be read in that fashion"
verdicts.note: DMR Books, Deuce Richardson, 10 May 2019; raw page reached live, HTTP 200. First limb verbatim: "His stories are 'engineered,' in that seemingly inconsequential details will have consequences later on." The mystery limb is over-generalised twice over: the page limits it to "Virtually every tale of his from the '70s-on" and immediately qualifies "though the mystery in each is usually not of the 'whodunit?' type."

verdicts.trueWording: "there comes a line of just two words: 'Silk nodded.' And it's absolutely heartbreaking."
verdicts.note: Lawrence Person, "Gene Wolfe, RIP", 16 April 2019; raw post reached live, HTTP 200. Every limb on the page: "In Return to the Whorl, there comes a line of just two words: 'Silk nodded.' And it's absolutely heartbreaking." The tragedy is framed as the work's - "He comes back thinking he's failed. The great tragedy of the work is that he hasn't" - naming The Book of the Short Sun, of which Return to the Whorl is the volume that carries the line, so "delivers its central tragedy" holds.

verdicts.trueWording: "Readers will also find a helpful lexicon for the obscure words and expressions"
verdicts.note: WolfeWiki page for The Castle of the Otter; raw page reached live, HTTP 200. Quote verbatim inside the SFBC jacket blurb, which also carries the names limb: "you'll read Wolfe's own explanation of how he named his characters and what the names mean." The page's Contents list confirms both essays, though the second is titled in full "Onomastics, the Study of Names (1982)" - the claim shortens it to 'Onomastics'. "Words Weird and Wonderful (1982)" is exact.

verdicts.unsupportedLimb: that Wolfe acknowledges the Borges and Crowley homages - those are the interviewer's attributions, and Wolfe answers only on M. R. James
verdicts.trueWording: "I'd say that the depth of my parodic streak is about five and half feet."
verdicts.note: SF Site, "A Magus Of Many Suns: An Interview With Gene Wolfe", Nick Gevers, January 2002, via the Wayback capture in the URL (HTTP 200, raw HTML). The joke is verbatim - and note the page reads "five and half feet", without the "a" the claim's paraphrase inserts. The homage limb is misattributed: it is Gevers who writes "some obvious (Borges in 'Useful Phrases') but others more fugitively so (John Crowley in 'The Haunted Boardinghouse', M. R. James in 'One-Two-Three For Me')". Wolfe's entire reply on that point is "I'm amazed that you saw M. R. James in 'One-Two-Three For Me.' You're very perceptive." - and an editorial insert adds that even that was pointed out by someone else. Wolfe acknowledges no Borges or Crowley homage on this page.

verdicts.trueWording: "the world we're immersed in is one we begin to inhabit much as the characters do"
verdicts.note: Gerlach 1999, printed p. 155; PDF fetched as binary from gwern.net (HTTP 200, 148,965 bytes) and text-extracted. Quote verbatim. The contrastive limb is supported by the same paragraph and the one before it: "clues are so sparse the reader will focus elsewhere" and "only occasionally is a clue given to invoke again the issue of who the gods are or where this world is" - i.e. no explanatory overview. One paraphrase drift worth recording: Gerlach writes "world"/"whorl", not "city", though his supporting detail is civic ("recurring street names").

verdicts.trueWording: "clues are so sparse the reader will focus elsewhere. Most of us focus on the plot"
verdicts.note: Gerlach 1999, printed p. 155, same extracted PDF. Quote verbatim and both limbs on the page: the world question does predominate early ("Although questions about this world this may predominate early") and the attention moves to plot ("Most of us focus on the plot, as we follow the protagonist, Patera Silk"). Page cite p. 155 is correct.

verdicts.trueWording: "This world is dense and intricate, rich in detail, with recurring street names"
verdicts.note: Gerlach 1999, printed p. 155, same extracted PDF. Quote verbatim, and the recurring-street-names limb is in the same sentence, which continues "new weapons - a needler, for instance, the equivalent of a .22 pistol." Page cite correct.

verdicts.unsupportedLimb: "rather than by coining new ones" - the same article cites Wolfe's coinages
verdicts.trueWording: "Words we're familiar with are applied in unusual, usually comical ways"
verdicts.note: Gerlach 1999, sentence spanning printed pp. 154-155, same extracted PDF; quote verbatim and the page cite is right. The repurposing limb is exactly Gerlach's ("'Mainframe' seems to be the place you go when you die"). But the exclusive limb is not on the page and is cut against by it: Gerlach discusses coined terms directly - "Terms like 'shadeup' and 'shadedown' are different, too" - and uses "whorl", "needler", "manteions", "chems" and "taluses" as the article's own vocabulary. Wolfe estranges by both routes here, not by repurposing instead of coining.

verdicts.unsupportedLimb: "with no narrator announcing the correction" - Gerlach never addresses how or whether the change is announced
verdicts.trueWording: "subsequent volumes offer a truer picture" of the Outsider in the prefaces
verdicts.note: Gerlach 1999, printed p. 159 (cite correct), same extracted PDF. Quote verbatim, and the revision mechanism is fully evidenced: the preface "God, Persons, and Animals Mentioned in the Text" before volume 2 calls the Outsider "the minor God who enlightened Silk", the volume 3 preface "the god of the broken and the disparaged whose realm lies outside the Whorl", and volume 4 "the god of gods". What the page does not carry is the narratorial claim - Gerlach simply quotes the three successive entries and calls the shift "perhaps the most delicious irony of all"; he says nothing about a narrator announcing or failing to announce it. Second, smaller stretch: he names prefaces to volumes 2, 3 and 4 only, not one "bound into each volume".

verdicts.trueWording: "The text encourages the reader to develop hypotheses about who the Outsider is from minimal clues"
verdicts.note: Gerlach 1999, printed p. 158 (cite correct), same extracted PDF. Quote verbatim; the full sentence continues "going beyond Dr. Crane's skepticism", and the preceding paragraph supplies the minimal evidence (Crane's Wernicke's-area diagnosis, the mud passage, the scaffold vision). Every limb supported.

verdicts.trueWording: Silk "does not question whether the Chenille he knows could be possessed"
verdicts.note: Gerlach 1999, printed p. 157 (cite correct), same extracted PDF. Quote verbatim. The gap limb is on the page in the adjoining clauses: "his concerns about the nature of his world are not those of the reader", "he accepts the concept of a god talking to him, because he has been raised to know the world as one that these gods rule", and the mechanism is stated positively as the characters' own view - "The reader is constantly tricked into accepting Silk's position ... because that's how everyone within the novel sees them" - against the reader's "humor of knowing that a theophany such as this cannot be exactly as Silk sees it." Gerlach never uses the phrase "narratorial comment", but he does locate the effect in the character's acceptance rather than in any narratorial gloss.

verdicts.trueWording: the three Soldier novels "begin with the same contrivance: an archeological discovery, an ancient scroll, with an introduction by Wolfe posing as translator"
verdicts.note: Farrell, "The Distant Suns of Gene Wolfe", First Things, April 2007; PDF fetched as binary from gwern.net (HTTP 200, 129,299 bytes) and text-extracted. Quote verbatim, and all three novels are named in the same sentence - Soldier of the Mist (1986), Soldier of Arete (1989), Soldier of Sidon (2006) - with the found-manuscript apparatus quoted at length after it (the urn of papyrus scrolls in the British Museum basement). Correction to the citation, not to the claim: the passage sits on printed p. 28 (running head "28 FIRST THINGS"), not p. 29 as the record states.

verdicts.trueWording: "Soldier of Sidon reads like a fictional travelogue through ancient Egypt"
verdicts.note: Farrell, First Things, April 2007, printed p. 29 (running head "APRIL 2007 29" - cite correct), same extracted PDF. Quote verbatim; the full sentence reads "Like its earlier installments. Soldier of Sidon reads like a fictional travelogue through ancient Egypt - an Egypt that more than two thousand years ago was already ancient - and Latro, with his new wife at his side, marvels at the many sights." Every limb supported.
